SAME SCALE: When attacker and target are the same scale, no modifier applies. X-wing vs TIE Fighter, stormtrooper vs Rebel soldier — all resolved at base stats.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS:
- Infantry need speeder-scale or walker-scale weapons (rocket launchers, turret-mounted guns, proton torpedo launchers) to damage vehicles.
- Starfighters struggle to damage capital ships with laser cannons but can use proton torpedoes (which have capital-scale damage ratings).
- Capital ship turbolasers are devastating if they hit a starfighter but have great difficulty tracking such small, fast targets.
- A character hiding behind cover is practically impossible for a Star Destroyer to target directly.

SPECIAL CASES:
- Proton torpedoes and concussion missiles are rated at a higher scale than the ship firing them. An X-wing's proton torpedoes deal Starfighter-scale 9D damage, which converts favorably against capital ships.
- Some weapons have variable settings or are designed to operate across scales.
- The GM may adjust scale modifiers for dramatic situations (the Death Star trench run, for example, forced capital-scale defenses to fight at starfighter scale due to the confined space).

chunks.title: Astrogation & Hyperspace
chunks.text:
Hyperspace travel is the primary means of crossing the vast distances between star systems in the Star Wars galaxy. The Astrogation skill (under Mechanical) governs the calculation of safe hyperspace routes.

HYPERSPACE BASICS: Hyperspace is an alternate dimension that allows faster-than-light travel. Ships equipped with a hyperdrive can enter hyperspace and cross the galaxy in hours or days rather than the millennia it would take at sublight speed. However, hyperspace travel is not without risk — gravity wells from stars, planets, and other massive objects create dangerous obstacles that must be navigated around.

ASTROGATION DIFFICULTIES:
- Well-traveled, pre-calculated route (Coruscant to Corellia, etc.): Very Easy (5) to Easy (10). These routes are stored in the ship's nav computer. The astrogator is essentially verifying and loading a known course.
- Moderately traveled route with current charts: Moderate (15). The route is known but may need adjustments for current conditions.
- Lightly traveled or outdated route: Difficult (20). The astrogator is working with incomplete or old data and must compensate.
- Unknown route, calculating from scratch: Very Difficult (25) to Heroic (30). The astrogator must plot an entirely new course using sensor data and stellar cartography. Extremely dangerous.
- Emergency jump (no calculations): Special. The ship jumps blindly into hyperspace. No Astrogation roll is made. The GM rolls secretly to determine what happens — the ship may arrive safely (unlikely), arrive off-course, collide with a celestial body, or be pulled out of hyperspace by a gravity well.

NAV COMPUTER: Most ships have a nav computer that stores pre-calculated routes and assists with new calculations. Using a nav computer reduces the difficulty by one level. Some small ships (like basic TIE fighters) lack nav computers entirely. Astromech droids (R2 units) can function as nav computers for starfighters, storing multiple jump coordinates and assisting with calculations (+1D to Astrogation).

HYPERDRIVE MULTIPLIER: A ship's hyperdrive has a speed rating expressed as a multiplier. The lower the multiplier, the faster the ship:
- x0.5: Extremely fast, heavily modified (Millennium Falcon).
- x1: Fast, military-grade (X-wing, Star Destroyer).
- x2: Standard civilian freighter speed.
- x3: Slow, older or cheaper models.
- x4+: Very slow, outdated vessels.
Travel time is calculated by multiplying the base travel time for a route by the hyperdrive multiplier. A trip that takes 10 hours at x1 takes 20 hours at x2, 5 hours at x0.5, etc.

HYPERSPACE MISHAPS: Failing an Astrogation roll can have serious consequences depending on how badly the roll is missed:
- Failed by 1-5: The ship is pulled out of hyperspace prematurely and must recalculate. Minor delay.
- Failed by 6-10: The ship arrives significantly off-course, potentially in an unexpected and dangerous location.
- Failed by 11-15: The ship suffers a close encounter with a gravity well, taking damage to the hull and/or hyperdrive. Repairs needed.
- Failed by 16+: Catastrophic collision or hyperdrive explosion. The ship may be destroyed or the crew killed.

GRAVITY WELL PROJECTORS: The Empire uses Interdictor cruisers equipped with gravity well projectors that simulate the mass of a planet, pulling ships out of hyperspace or preventing them from jumping. Ships caught in an artificial gravity well must either destroy the Interdictor, move out of range, or fight their way clear.

HYPERSPACE TRAVEL TIMES: Travel between nearby systems in the same sector typically takes 1-12 hours at x1. Cross-galaxy trips (Core Worlds to Outer Rim) can take several days at x1. The GM sets exact travel times based on narrative needs, using the hyperdrive multiplier to differentiate between fast and slow ships.

chunks.title: Character Advancement
chunks.text:
Characters in Star Wars D6 improve over time by spending Character Points earned during play. Advancement is gradual and meaningful, with characters slowly becoming more competent and powerful.

IMPROVING SKILLS: To improve a skill by one pip (+1), the character must spend Character Points equal to the number of dice currently in the skill. For example:
- Improving Blaster from 4D to 4D+1 costs 4 Character Points.
- Improving Blaster from 4D+1 to 4D+2 costs 4 Character Points (still 4 dice, pips don't count).
- Improving Blaster from 4D+2 to 5D costs 4 Character Points.
- Improving Blaster from 5D to 5D+1 costs 5 Character Points.
Skills increase one pip at a time: +0 becomes +1, +1 becomes +2, +2 becomes the next full die.

TRAINING TIME: Improving a skill also requires training time:
- If the character has a teacher with a higher skill level: Training takes one day per Character Point spent.
- If the character is self-teaching (no teacher): Training takes one week per Character Point spent, AND the cost doubles. So improving from 4D to 4D+1 without a teacher costs 8 CP instead of 4, and takes 8 weeks.
- If the character used the skill successfully in a dramatic or critical situation during the adventure: No training time is required (the experience itself is the training). This is a popular option that keeps the game moving.

IMPROVING ATTRIBUTES: Attributes can be improved, but at much greater cost. To improve an attribute by one pip, the character must spend Character Points equal to 10 times the current number of dice in the attribute. For example:
- Improving Dexterity from 3D to 3D+1 costs 30 Character Points.
- Improving Dexterity from 3D+1 to 3D+2 costs 30 CP.
- Improving Dexterity from 3D+2 to 4D costs 30 CP.
- Improving Dexterity from 4D to 4D+1 costs 40 CP.
Attribute improvement also requires extensive training time (at least one month with a teacher, several months without). Improving attributes is a long-term investment. Note that improving an attribute does NOT retroactively improve skills based on that attribute — skills are tracked independently once they have been raised above the base attribute.

LEARNING NEW SKILLS: A character can learn a new skill they do not possess by allocating the first pip. The cost is the base attribute's die code in Character Points, and requires a teacher or appropriate training materials. For example, learning Astrogation when you have Mechanical 3D costs 3 CP to go from Mechanical 3D (default) to Astrogation 3D+1.

FORCE SKILL ADVANCEMENT: Force skills (Control, Sense, Alter) advance like regular skills when the character has a teacher. Without a teacher, the CP cost is DOUBLED (and finding a Force teacher in the Empire era is extremely difficult). Learning new Force powers requires having the appropriate Force skill(s) at the required level and spending time in training or meditation.

LEARNING FORCE POWERS: Each individual Force power must be learned separately. The character needs the prerequisite Force skill(s) and must spend time training (typically a few days with a teacher, weeks without). Some powers are considered basic and can be learned relatively easily, while advanced powers (like Battle Meditation) may require very high Force skill levels and extended training.

SPECIALIZATIONS: Characters can take specializations within skills, narrowing their focus for increased ability. A specialization costs half the normal CP to improve but only applies to a specific subset of the skill. For example, 'Blaster: Heavy Blaster Pistol' would be cheaper to improve than general Blaster but only applies when using heavy blaster pistols.

chunks.title: Gamemaster Guidelines
chunks.text:
The Gamemaster (GM) in Star Wars D6 is the storyteller, referee, and creative engine of the game. The system is designed to be fast, flexible, and cinematic, giving the GM wide latitude to create exciting adventures that capture the spirit of Star Wars.

SETTING DIFFICULTY NUMBERS: The GM's most frequent task is setting difficulty numbers for player actions. The key principle is to match the difficulty to the drama and plausibility of the situation, not to rigidly simulate physics. Ask yourself: 'In a Star Wars movie, how hard would this be for the character attempting it?' A hotshot pilot threading through an asteroid field should face a Difficult or Very Difficult piloting check — challenging but achievable for a skilled character. Reserve Heroic difficulties for truly legendary moments.

Guidelines for difficulty:
- If failure would not be interesting or dramatic, do not require a roll. Just let the character succeed.
- If both success and failure would create interesting story outcomes, set the difficulty at Moderate to Difficult.
- If only extraordinary effort should succeed, set it at Very Difficult or Heroic.
- Use opposed rolls when two characters compete directly.

AWARDING CHARACTER POINTS: CP awards are the primary lever for pacing character growth. Award 3-6 CP for routine sessions, 6-10 for eventful sessions, and 10-15 for climactic adventures. Bonus CP for exceptional roleplaying, clever problem-solving, or memorable moments encourage players to engage with the story.

AWARDING FORCE POINTS: Force Points should be awarded sparingly — 0-1 per adventure. A Force Point award recognizes a truly heroic, selfless, or dramatically pivotal action. Not every adventure needs to result in a Force Point award.

PACING: Star Wars stories move fast. Combat should be resolved quickly — the D6 system is designed for speed. If a combat encounter is dragging, escalate the stakes, introduce new elements, or resolve it narratively. Avoid long, grinding fights. Similarly, keep skill checks moving. One roll should usually resolve a situation; avoid requiring multiple rolls for the same task unless escalation is dramatically interesting.

THE STAR WARS TONE: The game should feel like Star Wars. Key tonal elements include:
- Good vs Evil with moral complexity and hope for redemption.
- Swashbuckling action and narrow escapes.
- Humor and banter amid serious stakes.
- The underdog fighting against overwhelming odds.
- Personal connections and relationships driving the story.
- The Force as a mystical, spiritual element — not just a power system.
- Consequences that matter but rarely feel punitive.

IMPROVISING: The D6 system excels at improvisation. When players do something unexpected, set a reasonable difficulty, have them roll the most appropriate skill, and narrate the result. You do not need a specific rule for every situation — the core mechanic (skill dice vs difficulty number) handles everything.

THE RULE OF FUN: When in doubt, choose the option that is most fun and most Star Wars. If a player attempts something awesome that is technically outside the rules, find a way to let them try. The dice will sort out the probability. If a rule gets in the way of a great story moment, bend or ignore the rule.

ADVENTURE DESIGN: Great Star Wars adventures feature a clear objective, rising tension, memorable NPCs (villains and allies), exotic locations, moral choices, and a climactic confrontation. Structure adventures in three acts: the setup (introduce the problem), the complications (things go wrong, stakes escalate), and the climax (the dramatic resolution). Leave room for player agency — the best adventures are shaped by player choices, not predetermined scripts.

NPC DESIGN: NPCs do not need full character sheets. Give important NPCs 3-5 key skills and attributes that are relevant to their role. Stormtroopers have Blaster 4D, Dodge 4D, Brawling 3D, and that is enough. Darth Vader has absurdly high stats in everything that matters. Supporting characters need just enough stats to fulfill their narrative purpose.

chunks.title: Common Situations
chunks.text:
Star Wars D6 handles a wide variety of common gameplay situations beyond standard combat. Here are detailed rules for frequently encountered scenarios.

CHASES: Vehicle and foot chases use a series of opposed rolls between the pursuer and the quarry. Each round of the chase, both sides roll their relevant piloting or movement skill. The GM describes obstacles, terrain, and hazards that require additional rolls or increase difficulty.

Vehicle Chase Structure:
1. Both sides roll their piloting skill (plus vehicle maneuverability).
2. The winner gains or closes distance. The margin of success determines how much ground is gained or lost.
3. The GM introduces obstacles each round: sharp turns (Moderate piloting check), narrow passages (Difficult), oncoming traffic (Very Difficult), etc. Failure on an obstacle roll may mean a crash, a forced detour, or damage.
4. The chase ends when one side escapes (opens enough distance), is caught (closes to engagement range), crashes, or gives up.
5. Weapons can be fired during chases, but firing while piloting incurs multiple action penalties.

Foot chases work similarly, using running speed (based on Move rate) and opposed Stamina or relevant skill rolls.

SNEAKING AND STEALTH: Stealth situations use Sneak (to move silently) and Hide (to remain concealed) against the opposition's Search or Perception.
- Sneak vs Search: If the sneaking character's Sneak roll exceeds the searcher's roll, they remain undetected. The GM may set a base difficulty if no one is actively searching.
- Hide vs Search: Used when a character is stationary and concealed. Environmental factors modify both rolls: darkness gives +1D to +2D to Hide/Sneak, open terrain gives +1D to +2D to Search.
- Cover and concealment: Dense foliage, crowds, cluttered rooms, and similar environments reduce Search difficulty by 5-10 or add +1D to +2D to Sneak/Hide.

SOCIAL ENCOUNTERS: Social skills resolve non-combat conflicts:
- Con vs Perception or Willpower: Lying and deception. The Con artist rolls against the target's Perception (to detect the lie) or Willpower (to resist believing it). Specific, detailed lies may be easier to spot (+5 to detection difficulty) but more convincing if believed.
- Persuasion vs Difficulty: Convincing someone through logic, charm, or emotional appeal. The difficulty depends on how reasonable the request is: Very Easy for something the target already wants to do, Moderate for neutral requests, Difficult for things against the target's interests, Very Difficult for things actively harmful to the target.
- Bargain vs Bargain: Haggling and negotiation. Both sides roll; the winner gets better terms. The margin of success determines how favorable the deal is.
- Intimidation vs Willpower: Coercing through threats. Success means the target is frightened and compliant (at least temporarily). Failure may make the target angry, hostile, or dismissive.
- Command vs Willpower: Ordering subordinates or inspiring troops. Works best on those who recognize the character's authority. More effective in military contexts.

SLICING COMPUTERS: Computer Programming/Repair is the skill for hacking (slicing) into computer systems.
- Basic access (public terminal): Very Easy (5).
- Restricted files on an unsecured system: Easy (10).
- Standard security system: Moderate (15).
- Military-grade encryption: Difficult (20).
- Imperial Intelligence network: Very Difficult (25) to Heroic (30).
Slicing takes time: simple tasks are one round, complex tasks may take minutes or hours. Failing by a large margin may trigger alarms.

PICKING LOCKS AND SECURITY BYPASSING: The Security skill is used to bypass physical locks, electronic locks, alarm systems, and security measures.
- Simple lock: Very Easy (5).
- Standard electronic lock: Easy (10) to Moderate (15).
- High-security lock (bank vault, military installation): Difficult (20) to Very Difficult (25).
- Cutting-edge Imperial security: Heroic (30+).
Security tools (lockpicks, electronic bypass kits) may add +1D to +2D to the roll. Without tools, the difficulty increases by +10 or more.

REPAIRS: Repairing damaged equipment, vehicles, and ships uses the appropriate repair skill:
- Cosmetic/minor damage: Easy (10), takes minutes.
- Moderate damage: Moderate (15), takes hours.
- Heavy damage: Difficult (20), takes a day or more.
- Severe damage/near-destruction: Very Difficult (25), takes days and requires parts.
Having a full workshop and spare parts reduces difficulty by one level. Field repairs without proper tools increase difficulty by one level.
